newsitem.title: USA: Fed came close to tightening in Sept - sources.
newsitem.headline: Fed came close to tightening in Sept - sources.

text.p: The Federal Reserve nearly raised short-term interest rates in September and has not shelved that option for the coming months, Fed sources said.
"They came very close to raising rates around the time of the September (24) meeting," a Fed source told Reuters, referring to the next-to-last Federal Open Market Committee meeting.
The source said a number of Fed bank presidents -- such as San Francisco's Robert Parry, the most senior president in the Fed system -- had been favoring a rate hike at the time.
Concern that inflationary pressures would eventually emerge as a result of tight labor markets was the main argument in favor of a rate hike, the source added.

The September 24 FOMC meeting was held just days after eight of the 12 Fed district banks requested an increase in the 5.0-percent discount rate. Three of those banks had sought a 50-basis-point hike.
Another Fed source said Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan had considered, shortly before that meeting, raising the federal funds rate 50 basis points to 5.75 percent from 5.25.
That source said Greenspan favored a 50-basis point hike in part because a sharp move was more likely to prevent a pronounced Treasury market selloff.
Fed leaders have expressed sensitivity to market reaction, especially in light of a market slump that followed its string of small, gradual rate hikes in 1994.
The possibility of a Treasury market overreaction to a rate change "remains a concern" at the Fed, that source said.
Such concern was highlighted in the minutes of the September 24 meeting, released on Friday.
"A delay in adjusting monetary policy... was further supported by the possibility of an excessive reaction in financial markets," the minutes showed.
But the source said a larger rate hike would have required persuasive evidence that tight labor markets are actually feeding through into higher inflation, as they have historically.
Despite an unemployment rate below 5.9 percent since September 1994, few signs of higher inflation are evident.
The source also asserted that financial markets tend to misinterpret the Fed's policy goals.

"The long-term goal remains price stability," the source said, while stressing the Fed not only remains vigilant against signs of incipient inflation but also aims at driving the underlying inflation trend lower.
The September meeting minutes showed the FOMC maintained the bias toward tightening first put in place at the July 2-3 meeting and sustained after the August 20 meeting.

For the third straight meeting, Minneapolis Fed President Gary Stern dissented from the majority, favoring "modestly more restrictive policy," which Fed-watchers interpreted as an immediate 25-basis point fed funds rate hike.
The Fed last met on November 13, at which time it left both the fed funds and discount rates unchanged, as they have been since January 31.
